El bloque anterior enseñó a decir con pr: The previous block taught you to say precisely what is true and what a set is. This block builds the numbers, one after another: first the ones for counting, and with each topic a new kind is added when the previous one falls short. We start with how the naturals are written and compared, which looks trivial and is the idea that makes a calculator work.
Todo empieza aquí. Los <strong>números n: Everything starts here. The natural numbers are the ones for counting objects: $1, 2, 3, 4, \dots$ They never run out: however large one is, you can always add 1 and get a bigger one. That infinite set is called $\mathbb{N}$.
La letra hueca $\\mathbb{N}$ se dice <st:
The hollow letter $\mathbb{N}$ is said “N” and is the name of the set of natural numbers. The braces $\{\ \}$ are read “the set of”, and the three dots $\dots$ mean “and so on, with no end”.

Whole: “N is the set made up of zero, one, two, three, four, five, and so on”.

It is written with that doubled letter to tell it apart from any old n being used as an unknown. You will see the same idea with $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}$ as more numbers turn up.
El $0$ es un caso especial: durante sigl: $0$ is a special case: for centuries it was not considered a number, because nobody counts “zero sheep”. Today it is included in $\mathbb{N}$ because it is needed to write quantities such as 105 and because it is the natural starting point when counting.
Contar es más viejo que escribir. El <em: Counting is older than writing. The Ishango bone (Democratic Republic of the Congo, about 20,000 years old) has grouped notches that look like a tally. The Babylonians counted in base 60 (hence the 60 minutes and the 360°), the Romans with letters (MCMXLIV) and the Maya in base 20. The system we use today was born in India around the fifth century, travelled to the Arab world —where al-Khwarizmi explained it in a book that gave rise to the word algorithm— and reached Europe in 1202 with Fibonacci's Liber Abaci. It took three centuries to catch on.
Nuestro sistema es <strong>decimal</stro: Our system is decimal (ten symbols: 0-9) and positional: the same digit is worth one thing or another depending on where it is written. In $333$ the three threes are worth different things: three hundred, thirty and three.
Eso es justo lo que los números romanos: That is exactly what Roman numerals did not have: in XXX the three X's are worth ten each. That is why multiplying with Roman numerals is next to impossible, and with our system a ten-year-old does it.
Mueve cada rueda y observa cómo cada cif: Move each wheel and watch how each digit contributes its value according to the place it occupies.
Si subes la rueda de las centenas de 0 a: If you raise the hundreds wheel from 0 to 1, how much does the number grow? And if you raise the ten-thousands wheel by one?
El valor posicional es lo que hace que u: Place value is what makes a computer work. The machine only tells two states apart, so it counts in base 2: with 8 places (a byte) it reaches $2^8 = 256$ different values, and from there come the numbers from 0 to 255 in an IP address, the 256 shades of each colour on a screen and the famous 255-character limit of so many forms. The base changes, but the idea —each place is worth a power— is the same one you are using with units, tens and hundreds.
Ese «cuenta en base 2» se puede ver cons: That “counts in base 2” can be seen actually built. In [[maq-bits|the machines and languages block]] the eight switches of a byte are turned on and off by hand, and from there a whole computer is raised: first the gates, then the adder, and finally a machine that runs programs. Everything underneath is this place value with two symbols instead of ten.

Los naturales están <strong>ordenados</s: The naturals are ordered: given two of them, you can always say which is larger. The most useful way of picturing them is placed on a line, at equal intervals. The further right, the bigger.
Para comparar dos números escritos en ci: To compare two numbers written in digits there is an infallible rule: first count how many digits each one has (the one with more is larger); if they have the same number, compare digit by digit starting from the left.
$9\\,876$, porque empieza por 9 y el otr: $9{,}876$, because it starts with 9 and the other with 1
La primera cifra solo decide cuando los: The first digit only decides when the two numbers have the same number of digits. First you have to count digits.
$10\\,234$, porque tiene cinco cifras y: $10{,}234$, because it has five digits and the other has four
Cualquier número de cinco cifras es mayo: Any five-digit number is larger than any four-digit one: the smallest five-digit number, $10{,}000$, already beats the largest four-digit one, $9{,}999$.
Entre 7 y 8, ¿cuántos naturales hay? ¿Y: Between 7 and 8, how many naturals are there? And between 7 and 800? Do they ever run out to the right?
Arrastra el punto azul. Fíjate en que en: Drag the blue point. Notice that between two consecutive naturals there is no other natural: the naturals are a string of separate beads.
El punto solo puede posarse sobre los en: The point can only land on whole numbers: there is no such thing as “the natural between 3 and 4”.
Cuando un número es grande y no necesita: When a number is large and we do not need full precision, we round it. The rule: you look at the digit after the place you want to keep; if it is $5$ or more, you go up one unit; if it is $4$ or less, you leave it as it is. The rest is filled with zeros.
Localizar la cifra de las centenas: en $: Locate the hundreds digit: in $47{,}\underline{3}62$ it is the 3. Everything to its right, the 62, is going to disappear.
¿Qué cifra ocupa el lugar de las centena: Which digit occupies the hundreds place?

¿Qué cifra decide si se sube o se baja?: Which digit decides whether you go up or down?
Como $6 \\ge 5$, la centena sube una uni: Since $6 \ge 5$, the hundreds go up one unit: the 3 becomes 4. The digits to the right are replaced by zeros.
Con un 6, ¿se sube o se deja como está?: With a 6, do you go up or leave it as it is?
El caso que despista es el 9: redondear: The case that trips people up is the 9: rounding $2{,}951$ to the ten raises the 5 to 6 with no trouble, but rounding $2{,}995$ to the ten turns the 99 into 100 and gives $3{,}000$. It carries just as in an addition.
Cada cero ocupa un sitio y vale por él:: Each zero occupies a place and counts for it: 3,005 is three thousand and five. Without the zeros the 3 would fall in the hundreds.
Redondear 1 449 a las centenas mirando l: Rounding 1,449 to the hundreds by looking at the last digit
Se mira la cifra siguiente a la que se r: You look at the digit after the one you are rounding, the tens: 4, so 1,400. Looking at the 9 at the end leads to 1,500, which is further away.
1 999 a las centenas: truncado, 1 900; r: 1,999 to the hundreds: truncated, 1,900; rounded, 2,000. Truncating always goes down; rounding goes to the nearest.

Redondear no es «hacer trampa»: es una d: Rounding is not “cheating”: it is a decision with consequences. A supermarket that rounds every line of the receipt and one that rounds only the total can charge you different pennies for the same shopping, and that is why regulations fix when rounding happens. On a payslip or in a dividend distribution, the penny left over from rounding has to go somewhere, and deciding where is part of designing the system.
